claim: Goodyear's official retrospective states that the 1966 Le Mans-winning McLaren/Amon GT40 started on Firestones, found Goodyears better suited to the damp conditions, and switched to Goodyear during the race.
applicability: 1966 Le Mans GT40 supplier/event and wet-choice context.

claim: The same retrospective reports the Firestone-equipped McLaren GT40 losing chunks of tread on the Mulsanne at more than 210 mph in damp conditions before the switch.
applicability: Event-specific secondary retrospective; supports failure-mode research, not a universal speed threshold.

claim: A 1970 period Group 2 report states that the works 1.3-litre Escort used soft Dunlop 350-compound tires effectively on dry tracks, while the Mini was comparatively stronger when the track was wet.
provenanceLocation: Motor Sport, September 1970, 1001-1300 cc class discussion
applicability: Period vehicle/class/compound observation; no numerical grip or thermal coefficient.

claim: Goodyear's 1994 Formula One technical account says a 16 percent reduction in tire width reduced contained air volume and led teams to raise rear pressure from approximately 16 psi to 19 psi while the cavity shape was also changed.
provenanceLocation: Motor Sport, July 1994, quoted Goodyear engineering discussion
observable: inflation pressure and tire width/air volume
applicability: 1994 Goodyear Formula One construction only; do not transfer the pressures to other classes.

claim: The 1994 Formula One allocation was limited to seven sets per meeting, encouraging conservative compound recommendations to avoid blistering and insufficient inventory.
applicability: 1994 Formula One/Goodyear allocation and compound-selection context.

claim: Dunlop's official 1994 history says Le Mans was not especially abrasive in that configuration and describes a SARD Toyota/Dunlop specification developed to favor braking and cornering, with tire changes fitting within fuel stops.
provenanceLocation: Dunlop Motor Sport History, 1994 Le Mans section
applicability: 1994 Le Mans category/event context; later supplier retrospective.

claim: NASA-CR-3629 models free-rolling tire heat from cyclic stress/strain work in tire volume elements, then solves heat diffusion with wheel and runway boundary conditions.
applicability: Thermal-network architecture; aircraft absolute magnitudes are not transferable.

claim: NASA-CR-3629 compared calculated internal temperature distributions against buried thermocouples over varying loads, pressures, speeds and deflections and reported good agreement near normal rated conditions.
applicability: Validation-method evidence; does not validate Tire Lab coefficients by itself.

claim: In NASA's fixed-slip aircraft braking tests, cumulative tread wear varied approximately linearly with distance for a given condition, while wear rate increased with slip ratio.
observable: tread wear versus distance and slip ratio
applicability: Normalized wear architecture only; aircraft test magnitudes and life are not racing values.

claim: NASA-TN-D-7263 found runway surface material affected wear and tread temperature; at higher slip the slurry-seal tests could produce nonlinear tread chunking.
applicability: Surface- and incident-sensitive wear/failure mechanism only.

claim: A lighter-load comparison reduced inflation from 120 to 58 psi to match nominal deflection; in that test the pressure change reduced tread wear rate but had little effect on friction coefficient or tread temperature at essentially the same slip ratio.
applicability: Aircraft test and matched-deflection context only; demonstrates coupled load/pressure/deflection interpretation.

claim: NASA thermal tests changed deflection through pressure or load and found higher deflection increased sidewall-region temperature, while the cited tread-region tests showed much less sensitivity.
provenanceLocation: Results from Recent NASA Tire Thermal Studies, figure 6 discussion
applicability: Location-specific thermal-path evidence for aircraft tires; not a racing temperature target.

claim: A 1922 Goodyear/SAE abstract describes tire-temperature study across inflation, load, run length, stops, rim/tire size and design, identifying rapid flexing as a major heat source and pressure rise as one temperature-measurement method.
applicability: Early truck-tire mechanism and measurement chronology only.

claim: SAE 730183 reports measured vertical/lateral spring rates and traction parameters, with load and inflation pressure significantly affecting mechanical properties.
applicability: Truck-tire mechanism; no transfer of absolute stiffness to racing tires.

claim: SAE 2019-26-0360 treats ambient temperature, inflation pressure, speed, aging and cracks as interacting contributors to tire heat buildup and failure risk.
applicability: Aged high-speed road tires; qualitative coupling only.

claim: SAE 831027 distinguishes regulated-pressure rolling-loss tests from capped in-service tires and states that cold-to-equilibrium pressure increase can be estimated from physical principles across loads and initial pressures.
applicability: Pressure/temperature coupling architecture; examples are not racing targets.

claim: SAE J2704 defines a scalable method for measuring non-rolling normal force/deflection and gross footprint length/width for road-load modeling and comparative R&D.
applicability: Test-method evidence; no historical values.

claim: NASA-CR-3768 extends cyclic-deflection thermal modeling by superimposing heating from slip and braking stresses, then compares predictions with measurements across operating conditions.
applicability: Aircraft tire thermal architecture only.

claim: NASA-CR-4080 adds contact-scrubbing terms for yawed rolling and compares predicted internal temperatures across vertical deflection, inflation pressure and yaw conditions.
applicability: Aircraft tire thermal architecture only.

claim: McLaren's official heritage page places the F1 GTR in GT1 competition from 1995 and identifies BPR as its initiating series context.
applicability: Vehicle/series ontology and acquisition routing only.

claim: The RacingSportsCars BPR index supplies a structured 1994-1996 event chronology and links to result/program material for document acquisition.
applicability: Acquisition routing and event chronology, not tire physics.
